paragraphs.heading: The idea
paragraphs.text: The elastic-rebound theory is an idea from geology. It explains how energy is released during an earthquake. As Earth's crust deforms, the rocks that span the two opposing sides of a fault come under shear stress. They deform slowly, until their internal rigidity is exceeded. Then they separate in a rupture along the fault. The sudden movement releases the energy that had accumulated, and the rocks snap back almost to the shape they had at the start.

paragraphs.heading: Reid and San Francisco
paragraphs.text: After the great San Francisco earthquake of 1906, the geophysicist Harry Fielding Reid looked at how the ground surface along the San Andreas Fault had been displaced in the 50 years before the earthquake. He found evidence for 3.2 meters of bending over that period. His conclusion was that the quake must have come from the elastic rebound of strain energy that the rocks on both sides of the fault had stored. Later measurements made with the global positioning system largely support his theory as the basis of seismic movement.

paragraphs.heading: A locked fault
paragraphs.text: A fault can be active and yet locked. Its two sides are slowly moving in different directions, and elastic strain energy builds up in any rock mass next to them. The overall movement of the fault makes the rocks across the locked part take on more and more elastic deformation. This deformation may build at a rate of a few centimeters per year.

paragraphs.heading: The sudden break
paragraphs.text: When enough strain has accumulated to overcome the strength of the rocks, there is a sudden break. The rocks spring back toward their original shape as far as they can. That jolt is felt on the surface as an earthquake.

paragraphs.heading: A road across the fault
paragraphs.text: Picture a road built straight across a fault. It meets the fault trace at a right angle at a point where the fault is locked. When the sudden movement comes, the surface of the roadway is shifted.

paragraphs.heading: Where the energy goes
paragraphs.text: The stored energy leaves in three ways. Part of it is released as heat, part goes into altering the rock, and part travels away as a seismic wave. The mass of rock that was solid before is now divided between the two slowly moving plates.
